items.title: [al-monitor.com] Israelis vote in election that could end Netanyahu’s rule
items.content_html: Israelis began voting Tuesday in the first national election since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack, choosing all 120 members of parliament as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and an opposition bloc seeking to replace him. Final pre-election polls showed a close contest, with neither Netanyahu’s governing alliance nor the opposition expected to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority. Netanyahu faces scrutiny over the security failures preceding the Oct. 7 attack and his leadership through three years of regional wars. Campaign issues included whether to investigate those failures, the burden of military service and Israel’s political direction. Eisenkot has pledged an independent state inquiry, while Netanyahu’s government has rejected that demand. Israelis elect party lists rather than a prime minister directly. President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders and ask the candidate he judges best placed to form a coalition to do so. Reuters reported that the final tally was expected by Oct. 30 and official results on Nov. 4, after which coalition bargaining could take weeks.

items.title: [tass.com] Lula wins fourth Brazilian term as Bolsonaro seeks annulment
items.content_html: Brazil’s electoral court declared President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva the winner of Sunday’s runoff, giving him a fourth, nonconsecutive term after he overcame a first-round deficit against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula received 51.79% of valid votes to Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, a margin of about 4.4 million votes. It was Brazil’s first presidential runoff in which the first-round runner-up won, according to reported results. Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, refused to concede and said he would seek to annul the result, citing a Supreme Court justice’s last-minute, two-hour voting extension. Both campaigns had requested extra voting time; authorities later said the extension applied only to polling stations that were still open. Lula now faces a legislature with stronger conservative representation. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party holds 121 of 513 lower-house seats and 28 of 81 Senate seats, while public debt exceeds 80% of GDP. The official count is complete, and Lula is scheduled to take office on Jan. 1, 2027.

items.title: [firstpost.com] Brazil markets slide as Lula win revives fiscal concerns
items.content_html: Brazil-linked assets fell in early offshore trading Monday after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Investors had favored Bolsonaro, whom they viewed as more likely to pursue fiscal austerity and deregulation. An exchange-traded fund tracking Brazilian equities fell as much as 16% in Japan, while the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF dropped nearly 20% in overnight trading; currency derivatives signaled a possible decline of more than 10% in the real. These were early offshore moves, not Brazilian closing prices. Brazil’s electoral court gave Lula 51.79% of the vote to Bolsonaro’s 48.21%. Lula’s next term begins in January 2027. Public debt reached 82.9% of GDP in August, up more than 10 percentage points during Lula’s current term, while less than 8% of the federal budget is adjustable. Lula has pledged to protect social spending and raise the minimum wage. Investors are watching whether he can meet those pledges while stabilizing debt and inflation. Brazil’s benchmark interest rate was 13.75% and inflation was 4.6%. Inflation is not expected to reach the central bank’s 3% target until as late as 2029, Reuters reported. A consumption-tax overhaul approved in 2023 is also due to take effect in January, but the government has not disclosed its effective rate; independent analysts estimate it at about 28%.

items.title: [japantoday.com] Serbia’s student-backed list projected to win majority as Vučić concedes defeat
items.content_html: The student-backed Student List is projected to win a majority in Serbia’s parliament after former President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Sunday’s snap election, ending his Serbian Progressive Party’s 14-year dominance. Vučić said the list could take 135 to 140 of the 250 seats, against about 105 for his party; separate pollster projections put the Student List at 138 seats. The count remained preliminary. Turnout reached 67.6% by 7 p.m., the highest since Yugoslavia’s breakup in 1992. The election followed nearly two years of protests sparked by the November 2024 collapse of a railway-station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and failures of oversight, accusations the government rejected. The movement’s anti-corruption campaign drew support beyond students, and it entered the election with a slate of civil society candidates. With final results still pending, the Student List faces the task of forming a government without a single established leader. Its candidates have limited political experience. European Union officials offered help with rule-of-law and media reforms, while Vučić alleged foreign interference without providing evidence.

items.title: [AI Feed Curator] State of the Feed — Week of October 19–25, 2026
items.content_html:
This week the aggregator completed 7 runs, fetching an average of 1,418 articles per run and delivering an average of 85 quality-filtered articles per run. Across the week, ai-tech contributed the largest share of delivered articles at 126, followed by news (98), wellness (70), climate (60), science (56), local (51), homelab (44), design (40), homestead (20), outdoors (19), and scifi (10). Scoring uses a dimensional composite of quality, relevance, and locality weighted 0.25, 0.55, and 0.20 respectively, with relevance carrying the greatest weight in final selection.

Pipeline efficiency over the trailing 14 runs shows a mean noise-to-signal ratio of 2.31 articles fetched per article delivered, with a range of 0.96 to 3.28. The ratio sits near the middle of its observed range, and the upper end of the range indicates runs where a substantially larger share of fetched content was filtered out.

Feed changes this week include the addition of ABC News (listed twice in the intake log), AI as Normal Technology, 404 Media, and news releases. Two feeds reported errors during the period: Hacker News and Singularity Hub. Feed discovery surfaced three top candidates: blog.hmvh.net (score 73.2), Meshtastic Blog (score 64.8), and Machine Learning (score 64.7).

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
items.content_html: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] Forget the Live Aid image, Africa is only a broken continent in the minds of the west | Moky Makura
items.content_html:
Innovators and business leaders are driving progress across the continent-wide, but the ‘visibility gap’ prevents the rest of the world from truly seeing it

Thirty years ago, shortly after South Africa emerged from apartheid, I left London for Johannesburg in search of a better life. Not long afterwards, a friend who was preparing to visit from the UK called with an intriguing question: do they have ATMs in South Africa?

After I picked myself off the floor, I explained that not only did South Africa have ATMs, but in many respects its banking system was far more advanced than the one I had left behind in Britain. She was surprised and – dare I say – delighted that she wouldn’t have to lug a wad of cash around South Africa after all.
